data.title: Stupné – Žeravica, a hillfort and cult place in the Javorníky
data.excerpt: The rocky hill of Žeravica above Stupné, in the valley of the Papradňanka in the Javorníky mountains, is linked with a legend about a castle of the Krajčovci family that is said to have sunk into the ground. Test trenching in 1991 proved a hillfort of the Púchov culture here, and a hoard of Celtic coins and ornaments points to a cult place used for at least twenty-five centuries.

children.text: The village of Stupné, with the rocky hill of Žeravica, lies in the valley of the Papradňanka stream, which drains part of the territory forming the Javorníky mountains. Until now we have known little about the prehistoric occupation of the village of Stupné. According to Štefan Meliš, an old legend says that a castle once stood on Žeravica, owned by the Krajčovci family. Later the castle is said to have sunk into the ground. An entry in the village chronicle of Stupné says that metal objects (probably of bronze and iron) were found on the summit of Žeravica, where the castle stood.

The chronicler of the village – a teacher who began writing the chronicle in 1932 – recorded in it that old Stupné originally stood in the locality known as Spád, at the south-eastern foot of Žeravica. That is what the ancient folk legend says. Because the village descended from the locality of Spád down to the little river Papradňanka, to the place where it stands now, it was given the name Stupné. The name of the village has also gone through its own development. The first historical record of the village is from 1416, when it is mentioned as Stupničná. In 1467 it appears as Stupná, and from 1525 to the present day the name of the village is Stupné.

children.text: In 1991 Š. Meliš and F. Jandušík recovered several small sherds of the Roman period by means of a small test trench on the summit of Žeravica. They sent them to a specialist at the Považie Museum in Žilina, the archaeologist J. Moravčík. He confirmed that the sherds belonged to the people of the Púchov culture. Subsequently the members of the archaeological club in Považská Bystrica, together with the archaeologist J. Moravčík, carried out test trenching on Žeravica, where a dwelling with a floor paved with stones was identified; many sherds from broken vessels were also found. Further sherds were recovered by surface collection on the northern slope of the hill just below the summit. In this way they proved that there had been a hillfort on Žeravica. The acropolis of the hillfort (the highest-lying area) has terraced foundations some 140 m long, and 5–10 m wide. A further part of the hillfort, separated by a small saddle, lies in the woodland to the north-east.

children.text: The sherds recovered on Žeravica come from three periods. The graphite La Tène sherds are of the 1st century BC and the sherds of the Púchov culture of the period 0 – 400 AD; two sherds with wavy decoration, probably Slavic (8th – 9th century?), were also found. Beneath the foot of the crags, in the locality known as Spád, they also discovered the settlement below the hillfort (the suburbium). A large quantity of daub in the ploughed fields testifies to the dwellings that once stood there. The people of long ago recognised the strategic position of Žeravica and built a hillfort here. This fortified place was probably the centre of the whole valley.

At some point before 2009 a mass find was discovered on Žeravica, probably during landscaping work connected with the building of the Way of the Cross; it consisted of two circular ornaments and four coins of the later La Tène period. This find was studied by Július Frohlich in an article which concludes that “on the basis of their assessment it may be assumed that the mass find of Celtic coins and Púchov-culture ornaments is an exceptional votive offering, most probably dedicated at some time in the second to third quarter of the 1st century BC. Comparable ritual offerings of Celtic coins and precious-metal ornaments are known from several regions inhabited by Celtic tribes in the La Tène period. Further objects found individually at unspecified spots on this hill – a fragment of the terminal of a La Tène torc with the image of a human face with a third ‘eye’ on the forehead, an iron ritual axe, a boat-shaped fibula and silver coins of an unknown type – point to a long-lasting sacrificial function of the hill of Žeravica. The beginnings of the use of this place for the depositing of offerings may be assumed as early as at least the 5th century BC, while its cult character has been preserved in altered form down to the present day. This is documented by the Christian cross which now stands on this historically interesting hill. The archaeological artefacts from the site are thus exceptional testimony to the continuity of the spiritual dimension of this cult place, lasting at least twenty-five centuries, which the people of the Lusatian urnfields began to venerate from the turn of the Late Hallstatt phase HD and the Early La Tène phase LTA, that is, from the 5th century BC. The individual finds are at the same time testimony to the contacts which the inhabitants of north-western Slovakia maintained at that time with the southern, classical areas of contemporary Europe.”
